claim: Hyperventilation reliably provokes seizures in patients diagnosed with absence epilepsy.
source: Hyperventilation reliably provokes seizures in patients diagnosed with absence epilepsy.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation cited as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The mechanisms that enable hyperventilation to powerfully activate absence seizure-generating circuits remain entirely unknown.
source: Despite this predictable patient response, the mechanisms that enable hyperventilation to powerfully activate absence seizure-generating circuits remain entirely unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, representing the state of understanding prior to this study.

claim: Absence seizures in WAG/Rij rats are highly sensitive to arterial carbon dioxide.
source: By utilizing gas exchange manipulations and optogenetics in the WAG/Rij rat, an established rodent model of absence epilepsy, we demonstrate that absence seizures are highly sensitive to arterial carbon dioxide, suggesting that seizure-generating circuits are sensitive to pH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from gas exchange manipulations shown in Figures 1, 3, and 4.

claim: Seizure-generating circuits are sensitive to pH.
source: By utilizing gas exchange manipulations and optogenetics in the WAG/Rij rat, an established rodent model of absence epilepsy, we demonstrate that absence seizures are highly sensitive to arterial carbon dioxide, suggesting that seizure-generating circuits are sensitive to pH.
evidence: This is inferred from the CO2 sensitivity data, as CO2 affects pH.

claim: Hyperventilation consistently activated neurons within the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus.
source: Moreover, hyperventilation consistently activated neurons within the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, a structure implicated in seizure generation.
evidence: This is supported by cFos immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The intralaminar thalamus contains pH-sensitive neurons.
source: We show that intralaminar thalamus also contains pH-sensitive neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging and electrophysiology experiments in Figure 6D-H.

claim: Hyperventilation activates pH-sensitive neurons of the intralaminar nuclei to provoke absence seizures.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that hyperventilation activates pH-sensitive neurons of the intralaminar nuclei to provoke absence seizures.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Between 87% and 100% of all children diagnosed with childhood absence epilepsy produce spike-wave seizures upon voluntary hyperventilation.
source: Between 87% and 100% of all children diagnosed with the common genetic generalized epilepsy produce spike-wave seizures upon voluntary hyperventilation (Hughes, 2009; Ma et al., 2011; Sadleir et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hyperventilation serves as a powerful tool for diagnosing childhood absence epilepsy.
source: Indeed, hyperventilation serves as a powerful tool for diagnosing this childhood epilepsy (Adams and Lueders, 1981; Holowach et al., 1962; Sadleir et al., 2006; Watemberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical literature.

claim: No single genetic etiology drives absence epilepsy.
source: Remarkably, as no single genetic etiology drives absence epilepsy (Chen et al., 2013; Crunelli and Leresche, 2002; Helbig, 2015; Koeleman, 2018; Robinson et al., 2002; Xie et al., 2019), hyperventilation appears to recruit fundamental seizure-generating mechanisms shared virtually by all patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies of absence epilepsy.

claim: Hyperventilation appears to recruit fundamental seizure-generating mechanisms shared virtually by all absence epilepsy patients.
source: Remarkably, as no single genetic etiology drives absence epilepsy (Chen et al., 2013; Crunelli and Leresche, 2002; Helbig, 2015; Koeleman, 2018; Robinson et al., 2002; Xie et al., 2019), hyperventilation appears to recruit fundamental seizure-generating mechanisms shared virtually by all patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the high prevalence of hyperventilation-provoked seizures across genetically diverse patients.

claim: Exhalation of CO2 during hyperventilation causes hypocapnia.
source: Exhalation of CO2 during hyperventilation causes hypocapnia, a state of decreased arterial CO2 partial pressure (PaCO2), and respiratory alkalosis, a state of elevated arterial pH (Laffey and Kavanagh, 2002).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Exhalation of CO2 during hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis.
source: Exhalation of CO2 during hyperventilation causes hypocapnia, a state of decreased arterial CO2 partial pressure (PaCO2), and respiratory alkalosis, a state of elevated arterial pH (Laffey and Kavanagh, 2002).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Hyperventilation causes rapid arterial vasoconstriction.
source: Hyperventilation also causes rapid arterial vasoconstriction (Raichle and Plum, 1972) and increased cardiac output (Donevan et al., 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Hyperventilation causes increased cardiac output.
source: Hyperventilation also causes rapid arterial vasoconstriction (Raichle and Plum, 1972) and increased cardiac output (Donevan et al., 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Inspiration of 5% CO2 blunts hyperventilation-provoked spike-wave seizures in humans.
source: Recent work demonstrates that inspiration of 5% CO2 blunts hyperventilation-provoked spike-wave seizures in humans (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a human study.

claim: Respiratory alkalosis serves as the primary trigger for hyperventilation-provoked absence seizures.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that respiratory alkalosis serves as the primary trigger for hyperventilation-provoked absence seizures.
evidence: This is inferred from the CO2 supplementation data and prior human studies.

claim: Spike-wave seizures associated with absence epilepsy arise from hypersynchronous neural activity patterns within interconnected circuits between the thalamus and the cortex.
source: Spike-wave seizures associated with absence epilepsy arise from hypersynchronous neural activity patterns within interconnected circuits between the thalamus and the cortex (Avoli, 2012; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2009; Huguenard and McCormick, 2007; McCafferty et al., 2018; McCormick and Contreras, 2001; Meeren et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: The somatosensory cortex provides an initiating bout of synchronous activity that initiates a spike-wave seizure.
source: The crux of the prevailing model describing absence seizure generation includes an initiating bout of synchronous activity within the somatosensory cortex that recruits rhythmically active circuits in the thalamus (Meeren et al., 2002; Sarrigiannis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is the prevailing model in the field supported by citations.

claim: The extent to which thalamocortical circuits respond to shifts in pH during hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis is unknown.
source: The extent to which thalamocortical circuits respond to shifts in pH during hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Hyperventilation induced with hypoxia reliably evokes respiratory alkalosis in the WAG/Rij rat.
source: We first show that hyperventilation induced with hypoxia reliably evokes respiratory alkalosis and increases spike-wave seizure count in the WAG/Rij rat.
evidence: This is demonstrated by arterial blood gas measurements in Figure 3H.

claim: Hyperventilation induced with hypoxia increases spike-wave seizure count in the WAG/Rij rat.
source: We first show that hyperventilation induced with hypoxia reliably evokes respiratory alkalosis and increases spike-wave seizure count in the WAG/Rij rat.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ECoG recordings and seizure counts in Figure 1.

claim: When supplemented with 5% CO2 to offset respiratory alkalosis, hypoxia did not increase spike-wave seizure count.
source: When supplemented with 5% CO2 to offset respiratory alkalosis, hypoxia did not increase spike-wave seizure count.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Hypercapnia alone (high PaCO2) reduced spike-wave seizure count despite a robust increase in respiration rate.
source: Moreover, hypercapnia alone (high PaCO2) reduced spike-wave seizure count despite a robust increase in respiration rate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of brainstem respiratory centers to produce respiratory alkalosis during normoxia induces CO2-sensitive spike-wave seizures.
source: We also show that optogenetic stimulation of brainstem respiratory centers to produce respiratory alkalosis during normoxia induces CO2-sensitive spike-wave seizures.
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Respiratory alkalosis provokes spike-wave seizures.
source: Collectively, these results identify respiratory alkalosis as the primary seizure trigger in absence epilepsy following hyperventilation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data.

claim: Structures of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei are activated during respiratory alkalosis.
source: Finally, we show that structures of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei are both (1) activated during respiratory alkalosis and (2) pH sensitive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cFos immunoreactivity in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Structures of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei are pH sensitive.
source: Finally, we show that structures of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei are both (1) activated during respiratory alkalosis and (2) pH sensitive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging and electrophysiology in Figure 6D-H.

claim: Hypoxia reliably stimulates rapid breathing in rats.
source: Hypoxia reliably stimulates rapid breathing, blood alkalosis, and hypocapnia in rats (Basting et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hypoxia reliably stimulates blood alkalosis in rats.
source: Hypoxia reliably stimulates rapid breathing, blood alkalosis, and hypocapnia in rats (Basting et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hypoxia reliably stimulates hypocapnia in rats.
source: Hypoxia reliably stimulates rapid breathing, blood alkalosis, and hypocapnia in rats (Basting et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Relative to normoxia, spike-wave seizure count during hypoxia was nearly twofold higher (p = 4.5 × 10–7, n = 15).
source: Relative to normoxia, spike-wave seizure count during hypoxia was nearly twofold higher (p = 4.5 × 10–7, n = 15; Figure 1D, Table 1)
evidence: This is directly measured from ECoG recordings and quantified in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: Respiratory rate increased by 30% during hypoxia relative to normoxia (p = 1.6 × 10–5, n = 15).
source: respiratory rate increased by 30% (p = 1.6 × 10–5, n = 15; Figure 1E, Table 2)
evidence: This is directly measured from plethysmography recordings and quantified in Figure 1E and Table 2.

claim: The duration of individual spike-wave seizures was not altered by hypoxia (normoxia: 5.3 ± 0.4 s; hypoxia: 5.8 ± 0.4 s; p = 0.56, n = 15).
source: Whereas the duration of individual spike-wave seizures was not altered by hypoxia (normoxia: 5.3 ± 0.4 s; hypoxia: 5.8 ± 0.4 s; p = 0.56, n = 15, Table 3)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings and reported in Table 3.

claim: The frequency of individual spike-wave seizures was lower during hypoxia (normoxia: 7.6 ± 0.12 Hz; hypoxia: 5.8 ± 0.4 Hz; p = 4.7 × 10–5, n = 15).
source: the frequency of individual events was lower (normoxia: 7.6 ± 0.12 Hz; hypoxia: 5.8 ± 0.4 Hz; p = 4.7 × 10–5, n = 15, Table 4)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings and reported in Table 4.

claim: Between 62% and 84% of Wistar rats do not have seizures.
source: While between 62% (Vergnes et al., 1982) and 84% (Robinson and Gilmore, 1980) of Wistar rats do not have seizures
evidence: This is reported in cited literature.

claim: Wistar and WAG/Rij rats share the same genetic background.
source: as Wistar and WAG/Rij rats share the same genetic background (Festing, 1979)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In normoxia, seizures were absent in all four Wistar rats tested.
source: In normoxia, seizures were absent in all four Wistar rats we tested, consistent with the infrequent spike-wave seizure occurrence reported for this strain.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hypoxia induced hyperventilation, hypocapnia, and blood alkalization but did not provoke spike-wave seizures in Wistar rats.
source: Relative to normoxia in Wistar rats, hypoxia induced hyperventilation, hypocapnia, and blood alkalization but did not provoke spike-wave seizures (Figure 2; see Table 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2 and Table 5.

claim: Hypoxia primarily triggered arousal in Wistar rats.
source: Instead, hypoxia primarily triggered arousal in Wistar rats, as revealed in EEG spectrograms by the reduction in sleep-related frequencies.
evidence: This is observed in EEG spectrograms shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hypoxia-provoked spike-wave seizures are unique to seizure-prone rodent models.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that hypoxia-provoked spike-wave seizures are unique to seizure-prone rodent models, just as hyperventilation does not provoke absence seizures in otherwise healthy humans.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the differential response between WAG/Rij and Wistar rats.

claim: Hypoxia increased spike-wave seizure count by nearly twofold (p = 1.76 × 10–6, n = 9) in WAG/Rij rats.
source: As before, hypoxia increased spike-wave seizure count by nearly twofold (p = 1.76 × 10–6, n = 9; Figure 3B1 and C, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings and quantified in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: Hypoxia increased respiratory rate by 27% (p = 6.59 × 10–4, n = 9) in WAG/Rij rats.
source: and increased respiratory rate by 27% (p = 6.59 × 10–4, n = 9; Figure 3B3 and D, Table 2)
evidence: This is measured from plethysmography recordings and quantified in Figure 3D and Table 2.

claim: Supplementing hypoxia with 5% CO2 suppressed the spike-wave seizure response such that hypoxia/hypercapnia did not change spike-wave seizure count relative to normoxia (p = 0.18, n = 9).
source: In the same rats, supplementing hypoxia with 5% CO2 suppressed the spike-wave seizure response insofar that hypoxia/hypercapnia did not change spike-wave seizure count relative to normoxia (p = 0.18, n = 9; Figure 3E1 and F, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings and quantified in Figure 3F and Table 1.

claim: Hypoxia/hypercapnia produced a robust elevation in respiratory rate (p = 2.71 × 10–4, n = 9).
source: despite a predictable and robust elevation in respiratory rate (p = 2.71 × 10–4, n = 9; Figure 3E2, and G, Table 2)
evidence: This is measured from plethysmography recordings and quantified in Figure 3G and Table 2.

claim: Hypoxia decreased PaCO2 (p = 2.1 × 10–6 n = 6) in WAG/Rij rats.
source: Hypoxia decreased PaCO2 (p = 2.1 × 10–6 n = 6; Figure 3H2, Table 6)
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 3H2 and Table 6.

claim: Hypoxia alkalized the blood (p = 7.0 × 10–6, n = 6) in WAG/Rij rats.
source: and concomitantly alkalized the blood (p = 7.0 × 10–6, n = 6; Figure 3H3, Table 6)
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 3H3 and Table 6.

claim: Hypoxia decreased PaO2 (p = 6.0 × 10–6, n = 6) in WAG/Rij rats.
source: We also observed a decrease in PaO2 (p = 6.0 × 10–6, n = 6; Figure 3H1, Table 6).
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 3H1 and Table 6.

claim: Supplemental CO2 returned blood pH to normoxia levels (p = 0.008, n = 6).
source: Supplemental CO2 returned blood pH (p = 0.008, n = 6; Figure 3H3, Table 6)
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 3H3 and Table 6.

claim: Supplemental CO2 returned PaCO2 to normoxia levels (p = 0.42, n = 6).
source: and PaCO2 (p = 0.42, n = 6; Figure 3H2, Table 6) to normoxia levels.
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 3H2 and Table 6.

claim: Heightened respiratory rate in supplemental CO2 raised PaO2 (p = 00013, n = 6).
source: However, heightened respiratory rate in supplemental CO2 raised PaO2 (p = 00013, n = 6; Figure 3H1, Table 6).
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 3H1 and Table 6.

claim: Blood pH powerfully regulates spike-wave seizure activity.
source: Collectively, these data support the hypothesis that blood pH powerfully regulates spike-wave seizure activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective experimental data showing CO2/pH effects on seizures.

claim: The number of spike-wave seizures was lower during 5% CO2 relative to normoxia (p = 0.0028, n = 8).
source: Relative to normoxia, the number of spike-wave seizures was lower during 5% CO2 (p = 0.0028, n = 8; Figure 4B1, C, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings and quantified in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: Hypercapnia induced a powerful respiratory response (p = 3.78 × 10–5, n = 8).
source: hypercapnia also induced a powerful respiratory response (p = 3.78 × 10–5, n = 8; Figure 4B2,3 and 4D, Table 2)
evidence: This is measured from plethysmography recordings and quantified in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: 5% hypercapnia increased PaCO2 (p = 0.022, n = 6).
source: Blood gas measurements revealed that 5% hypercapnia increased PaCO2 (p = 0.022, n = 6; Figure 4E2)
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 4E2 and Table 6.

claim: 5% hypercapnia slightly acidified blood pH (p = 0.00063, n = 6).
source: and slightly acidified blood pH (p = 0.00063, n = 6; Figure 4E3, Table 6)
evidence: This is measured from arterial blood samples and quantified in Figure 4E3 and Table 6.

claim: The neural circuits that produce spike-wave seizures are CO2 sensitive.
source: These results provide further support for the hypothesis that the neural circuits that produce spike-wave seizures are CO2 sensitive, and thus pH sensitive.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing CO2 effects on seizures.

claim: Neither the mechanics of elevated ventilation nor increased arousal is sufficient to provoke spike-wave seizures.
source: Moreover, the results demonstrate that neither the mechanics of elevated ventilation nor increased arousal, is sufficient to provoke spike-wave seizures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hypercapnia increases ventilation but decreases seizures.

claim: Hypoxia lowers PaO2, which stimulates the carotid body.
source: In addition to inducing hyperventilation and hypocapnia, hypoxia also lowers PaO2 (see Figure 3H1), an effect that stimulates the carotid body, the principal peripheral chemoreceptor that initiates hyperventilation during hypoxic conditions (Lindsey et al., 2018; López-Barneo et al., 2016; Semenza and Prabhakar, 2018).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 3H1.

claim: The carotid body is the principal peripheral chemoreceptor that initiates hyperventilation during hypoxic conditions.
source: In addition to inducing hyperventilation and hypocapnia, hypoxia also lowers PaO2 (see Figure 3H1), an effect that stimulates the carotid body, the principal peripheral chemoreceptor that initiates hyperventilation during hypoxic conditions (Lindsey et al., 2018; López-Barneo et al., 2016; Semenza and Prabhakar, 2018).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Carotid body activity recruits neurons of the nucleus tractus solitarius that then excite neurons of the central respiratory pattern generator to drive a respiratory response.
source: Carotid body activity recruits neurons of the nucleus tractus solitarius that then excite neurons of the central respiratory pattern generator to drive a respiratory response (Guyenet, 2014; López-Barneo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Chemosensitive neurons of the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) are activated during an increase in PaCO2 and a consequent drop in arterial pH.
source: Under physiological conditions, chemosensitive neurons of the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), a brainstem respiratory center, are activated during an increase in PaCO2 and a consequent drop in arterial pH (Guyenet et al., 2016; Guyenet et al., 2019; Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015) that then stimulate respiration.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Optogenetic activation of RTN neurons in normoxia is sufficient to evoke a powerful hyperventilatory response that alkalizes the blood.
source: Optogenetic activation of RTN neurons in normoxia is sufficient to evoke a powerful hyperventilatory response that alkalizes the blood (Abbott et al., 2011; Souza et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior optogenetic studies.

claim: PaO2 remains stable (or is slightly elevated) during optogenetically induced respiration.
source: Importantly, PaO2 remains stable (or is slightly elevated) during optogenetically induced respiration.
evidence: This is inferred from the physiological effects of increased ventilation in normoxia.

claim: Laser stimulation during normoxia provoked spike-wave seizures (p = 0.002, n = 10).
source: Laser stimulation during normoxia provoked spike-wave seizures (p = 0.002, n = 10; Figure 5D, E1, and F, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings during optogenetic stimulation and quantified in Figure 5F and Table 1.

claim: Laser stimulation during normoxia increased ventilation (p = 0.019, n = 10).
source: and also increased ventilation (p = 0.019, n = 10; Figure 5E2,3, and 5G)
evidence: This is measured from plethysmography recordings during optogenetic stimulation and quantified in Figure 5G and Table 2.

claim: Laser stimulation during hypercapnia did not alter spike-wave seizure count (p = 0.86, n = 6).
source: Laser stimulation during hypercapnia in the same animals did not alter spike-wave seizure count (p = 0.86, n = 6; Figure 5H1 and I, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured from ECoG recordings during optogenetic stimulation with CO2 and quantified in Figure 5I and Table 1.

claim: Laser stimulation during hypercapnia induced a strong hyperventilatory response (p = 0.031, n = 6).
source: despite the induction of a strong hyperventilatory response (p = 0.031, n = 6; Figure 5H2,3, and 5J, Table 2)
evidence: This is measured from plethysmography recordings during optogenetic stimulation with CO2 and quantified in Figure 5J and Table 2.

claim: Respiratory alkalosis is necessary to provoke seizures during hyperventilation.
source: In sum, these results support the hypothesis that respiratory alkalosis is necessary to provoke seizures during hyperventilation and excludes carotid body activation as a contributing factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic experiments showing seizures only occur with alkalosis.

claim: Carotid body activation is not a contributing factor to hyperventilation-provoked seizures.
source: In sum, these results support the hypothesis that respiratory alkalosis is necessary to provoke seizures during hyperventilation and excludes carotid body activation as a contributing factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic experiments that bypass carotid body activation.

claim: Heightened cFos immunoreactivity was observed in the intralaminar nuclei following hypoxia.
source: Surprisingly, in rats exposed to hypoxia we observed heightened immunoreactivity in the intralaminar nuclei, a group of higher-order thalamic nuclei that, unlike first-order thalamic nuclei, do not receive peripheral sensory information (Saalmann, 2014; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cFos immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Intralaminar nuclei are higher-order thalamic nuclei that do not receive peripheral sensory information.
source: Surprisingly, in rats exposed to hypoxia we observed heightened immunoreactivity in the intralaminar nuclei, a group of higher-order thalamic nuclei that, unlike first-order thalamic nuclei, do not receive peripheral sensory information (Saalmann, 2014; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about thalamic organization supported by citation.

claim: cFos immunoreactivity was largely absent from first-order thalamic nuclei and cortex.
source: Indeed, cFos immunoreactivity was largely absent from first-order thalamic nuclei and cortex, and was blunted in rats treated with normoxia and hypoxia/hypercapnia (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cFos immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6B.

claim: cFos immunoreactivity was blunted in rats treated with normoxia and hypoxia/hypercapnia.
source: Indeed, cFos immunoreactivity was largely absent from first-order thalamic nuclei and cortex, and was blunted in rats treated with normoxia and hypoxia/hypercapnia (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cFos immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The number of cFos-positive cells within the intralaminar thalamic nuclei was highest following hypoxia [ANOVA: F (2, 6) = 31.59, p = 0.00019].
source: Immunoreactivity quantification revealed that the number of cFos-positive cells within the intralaminar thalamic nuclei was highest following hypoxia [ANOVA: F (2, 6) = 31.59, p = 0.00019, Figure 6C, Table 7].
evidence: This is quantified from cFos immunohistochemistry and shown in Figure 6C and Table 7.

claim: Extracellular alkalosis quickly and reversibly activated neurons of the intralaminar nuclei.
source: Recording fluorescence changes in brain sections revealed that extracellular alkalosis quickly and reversibly activated neurons of the intralaminar nuclei (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Alkaline bathing solutions evoke inward currents in intralaminar neurons.
source: An electrophysiological evaluation of pH sensitivity using voltage-clamp recordings (Vhold = –50 mV) showed that alkaline bathing solutions evoke inward currents in intralaminar neurons (Figure 6F and G, Table 7)
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 6F-G and Table 7.

claim: Alkaline-induced inward currents suggest that excitatory ion channels and/or receptors were activated.
source: suggesting that excitatory ion channels and/or receptors were activated
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of inward currents during alkaline conditions.

claim: Alkaline-induced inward currents appeared blunted in somatosensory thalamus and cortex.
source: Interestingly, alkaline-induced inward currents appeared blunted in other structures implicated in spike-wave seizure generation, such as somatosensory thalamus and cortex (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 6H and Table 7.

claim: Previous reports show blunted, macroscopic pH sensitivity in the somatosensory thalamus.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports of blunted, macroscopic pH sensitivity in the somatosensory thalamus (Meuth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Respiratory alkalosis activates pH-sensitive neurons of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei in the WAG/Rij rat.
source: Collectively, these results support the hypothesis that respiratory alkalosis activates pH-sensitive neurons of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei in the WAG/Rij rat.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the cFos, calcium imaging, and electrophysiology data.

claim: Hyperventilation-provoked seizures associated with absence epilepsy were first formally described in 1928 by Lennox.
source: Hyperventilation-provoked seizures associated with absence epilepsy were first formally described in 1928 by Lennox, 1928
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: No animal studies have attempted to resolve the physiological events that enable hyperventilation to reliably provoke spike-wave seizures.
source: and despite the clinical ubiquity of utilizing hyperventilation to diagnose the common form of childhood epilepsy, no animal studies have attempted to resolve the physiological events that enable hyperventilation to reliably provoke spike-wave seizures.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: Hyperventilation only provokes spike-wave seizures in seizure-prone, not generally seizure-free, rats.
source: With this model, we show that hyperventilation only provokes spike-wave seizures in seizure-prone, not generally seizure-free, rats.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing WAG/Rij and Wistar rat responses in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Supplemental CO2, by mitigating respiratory alkalosis, suppresses spike-wave seizures triggered by hyperventilation during either hypoxia or direct activation of brainstem respiratory centers.
source: We then show that supplemental CO2, by mitigating respiratory alkalosis, suppresses spike-wave seizures triggered by hyperventilation during either hypoxia or direct activation of brainstem respiratory centers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Supplemental CO2, by producing respiratory acidosis, suppresses spontaneous spike-wave seizures despite a compensatory increase in respiratory rate.
source: Moreover, supplemental CO2, by producing respiratory acidosis, suppresses spontaneous spike-wave seizures (i.e. those occurring during normoxia) despite a compensatory increase in respiratory rate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Spike-wave seizures are yoked to arterial CO2/pH.
source: These data demonstrate that spike-wave seizures are yoked to arterial CO2/pH.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data.

claim: Respiratory alkalosis activates neurons of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei in a CO2-dependent manner.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that respiratory alkalosis activates neurons of the intralaminar thalamic nuclei, also in a CO2-dependent manner
evidence: This is demonstrated by cFos data showing activation only during alkalosis, not during CO2-supplemented conditions (Figure 6).

claim: Activation of intralaminar neurons is pH sensitive.
source: activation of these neurons is also pH sensitive
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging and electrophysiology experiments in Figure 6D-H.

claim: Respiratory alkalosis activates pH-sensitive neurons of the intralaminar nuclei that in turn engage seizure-generating neural circuits to produce spike-wave seizures.
source: With these observations, we propose a working model wherein respiratory alkalosis activates pH-sensitive neurons of the intralaminar nuclei that in turn engage seizure-generating neural circuits to produce spike-wave seizures (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the collective findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Hyperventilation produces stereotypical EEG patterns in both healthy children and children with absence epilepsy.
source: Hyperventilation produces stereotypical EEG patterns in both healthy children and children with absence epilepsy (Barker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In healthy children, hyperventilation can evoke an EEG pattern known as hyperventilation-induced, high-amplitude rhythmic slowing (HIHARS) that is often associated with altered awareness.
source: In healthy children, hyperventilation can evoke an EEG pattern known as hyperventilation-induced, high-amplitude rhythmic slowing (HIHARS) that is often associated with altered awareness (Barker et al., 2012; Lum et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Electrographically, HIHARS is distinct from spike-wave seizures insofar the EEG lacks epilepsy-associated spikes and resembles slow-wave sleep.
source: Electrographically, HIHARS is distinct from spike-wave seizures insofar the EEG lacks epilepsy-associated spikes and resembles slow-wave sleep.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about EEG patterns.

claim: Age-dependence and behavioral similarities between HIHARS and absence seizures exist.
source: Nonetheless, age-dependence and behavioral similarities between HIHARS and absence seizures exist (Lum et al., 2002; Mattozzi et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: HIHARS and spike-wave seizures borrow from overlapping neural circuit mechanisms.
source: thereby supporting the hypothesis that HIHARS and spike-wave seizures borrow from overlapping neural circuit mechanisms (Mattozzi et al., 2021)
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citation.

claim: Human spike-wave seizures observed during hyperventilation are subtly different from those occurring spontaneously.
source: Indeed, while HIHARS and spike-wave seizures are clearly distinct EEG patterns, human spike-wave seizures observed during hyperventilation are subtly different from those occurring spontaneously (Sadleir et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Hyperventilation evokes HIHARS in cats.
source: Sherwin demonstrated that hyperventilation evokes HIHARS in cats (Sherwin, 1965)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior animal research.

claim: The stereotyped EEG pattern (HIHARS) requires an intact central lateral nucleus of the thalamus.
source: and that the stereotyped EEG pattern requires an intact central lateral nucleus of the thalamus (Sherwin, 1967)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior animal research.

claim: The central lateral nucleus belongs to the anterior group of the intralaminar nuclei.
source: Together with the central medial (CM) and paracentral thalamic nuclei, the central lateral nucleus belongs to the anterior group of the intralaminar nuclei (Saalmann, 2014)
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sherwin postulated that the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus are both chemoreceptive and capable of engaging widespread cortical activity.
source: Indeed, at the time Sherwin postulated that the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus are both chemoreceptive and capable of engaging widespread cortical activity (Sherwin, 1967).
evidence: This is a historical hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: The intralaminar nuclei are instrumental for provoking spike-wave seizures during hyperventilation.
source: We now postulate that these nuclei are also instrumental for provoking spike-wave seizures during hyperventilation.
evidence: This is the hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Interconnected circuits between the cortex and thalamus support the initiation and maintenance of generalized spike-wave seizures.
source: Decades of work have culminated in a canonical model wherein interconnected circuits between the cortex and thalamus support the initiation and maintenance of generalized spike-wave seizures (Avoli, 2012; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2009; Huguenard and McCormick, 2007; McCafferty et al., 2018; McCormick and Contreras, 2001; Meeren et al., 2002).
evidence: This is the prevailing model in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: The peri-oral region of somatosensory cortex provides the bout of hypersynchronous activity that initiates a spike-wave seizure.
source: By recording from multiple sites in the WAG/Rij rat, Meeren et al. (Meeren et al., 2002) concluded that the peri-oral region of somatosensory cortex provides the bout of hypersynchronous activity that initiates a spike-wave seizure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from prior research supported by citation.

claim: Cortical hyperactivity initiates spike-wave seizures.
source: Additional studies support the hypothesis that cortical hyperactivity initiates spike-wave seizures (Pinault, 2003; Pinault et al., 1998)
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Circuits between first-order thalamic nuclei and the reticular thalamic nucleus are sufficient to sustain rhythmic network activities, including those comparable to absence seizures.
source: Extensive work on acute brain slice preparations clearly demonstrates that circuits between first-order thalamic nuclei and the reticular thalamic nucleus are sufficient to sustain rhythmic network activities, including those comparable to absence seizures (Bal et al., 1995; Bal and McCormick, 1993; McCormick and Contreras, 2001; Krosigk von et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro studies supported by citations.

claim: It is becoming less clear how first-order thalamocortical neurons actively contribute to the maintenance of spike-wave seizures recorded in vivo.
source: While this model very likely accounts for rhythmicity in the acute brain slice preparation, it is becoming less clear how first-order thalamocortical neurons actively contribute to the maintenance of spike-wave seizures recorded in vivo (Huguenard, 2019; McCafferty et al., 2018).
evidence: This represents an evolving understanding in the field supported by citations.

claim: Most current models of spike-wave initiation and maintenance neglect the potential contribution of the intralaminar nuclei to seizure initiation and maintenance.
source: Moreover, most current models of spike-wave initiation and maintenance neglect the potential contribution of the intralaminar nuclei to seizure initiation and maintenance despite several observations to the contrary.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current models that the authors address.

claim: Stimulation of the anterior intralaminar nuclei was sufficient to evoke spike-wave seizures that outlasted the stimulus in cats.
source: By doing so in both lightly anesthetized (Jasper and Droogleever-Fortuyn, 1947) and unanesthetized (Hunter and Jasper, 1949) animals, the authors concluded that stimulation of the anterior intralaminar nuclei (i.e. central lateral, central medial, and paracentral nuclei) was sufficient to evoke spike-wave seizures that outlasted the stimulus
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical animal studies.

claim: Stimulation of first-order thalamic nuclei did not evoke spike-wave seizures, nor did it evoke seizure-like behaviors.
source: However, stimulation of first-order thalamic nuclei did not evoke spike-wave seizures, nor did it evoke seizure-like behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical animal studies.

claim: Lesions to the intralaminar nuclei abolish pharmacologically induced spike-wave seizures in Sprague-Dawley rats.
source: Consistent with these observations, lesions to the intralaminar nuclei abolish pharmacologically induced spike-wave seizures in Sprague-Dawley rats (Banerjee and Snead, 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior lesion studies.

claim: Seizures persist following lesions to first-order nuclei.
source: seizures persist following lesions to first-order nuclei
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior lesion studies.

claim: An EEG-fMRI study in human patients implicates the intralaminar nuclei in the initiation of spontaneous spike-wave seizures.
source: More recently, an EEG-fMRI study in human patients also implicates the intralaminar nuclei in the initiation of spontaneous spike-wave seizures (Tyvaert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a human neuroimaging study.

claim: Meeren et al. did not include intralaminar thalamic recordings during their study of spike-wave seizure propagation in the WAG/Rij rat.
source: Regrettably, (Meeren et al., 2002) did not include intralaminar thalamic recordings during their study of spike-wave seizure propagation in the WAG/Rij rat.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the methods of a prior study.

claim: Proposing the hypothesis that the intralaminar nuclei, not cortical structures, initiate spike-wave seizures seems premature.
source: Nonetheless, proposing the hypothesis that the intralaminar nuclei, not cortical structures, initiate spike-wave seizures, including those occurring spontaneously (i.e. not during hyperventilation), seems premature.
evidence: This is the authors' cautious interpretation of the evidence.

claim: Activation of cortically projecting intralaminar neurons during hyperventilation may recruit cortical structures to initiate spike-wave seizures.
source: Indeed, the possibility that activation of cortically projecting intralaminar neurons during hyperventilation recruits cortical structures to, in turn, initiate spike-wave seizures is equally plausible.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Activated intralaminar neurons may increase the excitability of the reticular thalamic nucleus, thereby lowering the threshold required for cortical input to spark a spike-wave seizure.
source: Alternatively, activated intralaminar neurons may increase the excitability of the reticular thalamic nucleus, a highly interconnected thalamic hub (Swanson et al., 2019), thereby lowering the threshold required for cortical input to spark a spike-wave seizure (see Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism proposed by the authors and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the intralaminar nuclei evokes robust excitatory and inhibitory responses in the ventral thalamic nuclei.
source: In support of this latter model, (Purpura and Cohen, 1962) demonstrated that electrical stimulation of the intralaminar nuclei evokes robust excitatory and inhibitory responses in the ventral thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: First-order thalamic neurons express several pH-sensitive ion channels and receptors.
source: First-order thalamic neurons express several pH-sensitive ion channels and receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ion channel expression.

claim: TASK-1 and TASK-3, with the HCN ion channel, collectively play a critical role in stabilizing the resting membrane potential of first-order thalamic neurons.
source: TASK-1 and TASK-3, two TWIK-related acid-sensitive potassium channels, with the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide–gated (HCN) ion channel, collectively play a critical role in stabilizing the resting membrane potential of first-order thalamic neurons (Meuth et al., 2003; Meuth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The opposing actions of TASK and HCN channels are simultaneously downregulated during extracellular acidification to yield no net effect on thalamocortical neuron membrane potential.
source: As extracellular acidification inhibits the activity of both channels, the opposing actions of TASK and HCN channels are simultaneously downregulated to yield no net effect on thalamocortical neuron membrane potential (Meuth et al., 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The opposing actions of TASK and HCN channels presumably stabilize thalamocortical membrane potential during alkaline conditions.
source: While not yet directly tested, the opposing actions of TASK and HCN channels also presumably stabilize thalamocortical membrane potential during alkaline conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the known properties of these channels.

claim: First-order thalamic nuclei are unlikely to support an active role in initiating hyperventilation-provoked spike-wave seizures.
source: Thus, while first-order thalamocortical neurons express pH-sensitive ion channels, these neurons are presumed to maintain stable membrane potentials during extracellular pH fluctuations. If true, then first-order thalamic nuclei are unlikely to support an active role in initiating hyperventilation-provoked spike-wave seizures.
evidence: This is inferred from the pH-buffering properties of first-order thalamic neurons.

claim: The extent to which higher-order thalamic nuclei express TASK and HCH channels remains unknown.
source: The extent to which higher-order thalamic nuclei express TASK and HCH channels remains unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Intralaminar neurons recruited during hyperventilation-mediated alkalosis may not reflect intrinsic pH sensitivity but may result from increased excitatory synaptic input.
source: Importantly, intralaminar neurons recruited during hyperventilation-mediated alkalosis may not reflect intrinsic pH sensitivity. Instead, activation of intralaminar neurons during alkalosis may result from increased excitatory synaptic input.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Intralaminar neurons receive significant, monosynaptic excitation from the midbrain reticular formation.
source: Intralaminar neurons receive significant, monosynaptic excitation from the midbrain reticular formation (Ropert and Steriade, 1981; Steriade and Glenn, 1982)
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: First-order thalamic nuclei only negligibly receive monosynaptic excitation from the midbrain reticular formation.
source: first-order thalamic nuclei only do so negligibly (Edwards and de Olmos, 1976)
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Several reticular nuclei are critically important for respiration.
source: Several reticular nuclei are critically important for respiration (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Smith et al., 2013)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: cFos expression was only observed during respiratory alkalosis (i.e. hypoxia) and not during hyperventilation associated with a normalized arterial pH (i.e. hypoxia-hypercapnia).
source: Notably, cFos expression was only observed during respiratory alkalosis (i.e. hypoxia) and not during hyperventilation associated with a normalized arterial pH (i.e. hypoxia-hypercapnia; c.f. Figures 3H and 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing cFos data across conditions in Figures 3H and 6B.

claim: If reticular-mediated excitation of intralaminar neurons plays a role in hyperventilation-provoked spike-wave seizures, then it does so only during conditions of respiratory alkalosis.
source: Thus, if reticular-mediated excitation of intralaminar neurons plays a role in hyperventilation-provoked spike-wave seizures, then it does so only during conditions of respiratory alkalosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the cFos data showing activation only during alkalosis.

claim: The synaptic terminals of intralaminar-projecting afferents may be pH sensitive.
source: Finally, the possibility that the synaptic terminals of intralaminar-projecting afferents are pH sensitive also warrants examination.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Solute carrier family transporters shuttle H+ and HCO3+ across neuronal membranes and are proposed to regulate seizures, including spike-wave seizures.
source: Notably, solute carrier family transporters shuttle H+ and HCO3+ across neuronal membranes and are proposed to regulate seizures, including spike-wave seizures (Cox et al., 1997; Sander et al., 2002; Sinning and Hübner, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Alkaline conditions enhance excitatory synaptic transmission, an effect attributed to Slc4a8, an Na+-driven Cl-/bicarbonate exchanger.
source: Alkaline conditions enhance excitatory synaptic transmission, an effect attributed to Slc4a8, an Na+-driven Cl-/bicarbonate exchanger (Sinning et al., 2011; Sinning and Hübner, 2013)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Slc4a8 is expressed in the presynaptic terminals of excitatory neurons, including those in the thalamus.
source: that is expressed in the presynaptic terminals of excitatory neurons, including those in the thalamus (Lein et al., 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The enhancement of synaptic excitation onto intralaminar neurons is a plausible mechanism to explain the large excitatory currents activated by alkalinization.
source: Thus, the enhancement of synaptic excitation onto intralaminar neurons remains a plausible mechanism to explain the large excitatory currents activated by alkalinization, as observed in Figure 6.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: The intralaminar nuclei appear particularly well suited to transduce alkalization into spike-wave seizures as pH sensitivity within these structures appears heightened relative to other nodes within the spike-wave seizure-generating circuitry.
source: The intralaminar nuclei appear particularly well suited to transduce alkalization into spike-wave seizures as pH sensitivity within these structures appears heightened relative to other nodes within the spike-wave seizure-generating circuitry (see Figure 6H).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative pH sensitivity data shown in Figure 6H.
